title: Indian-American Congressman Suhas Subramanyam Unveils Four-Bill National Data Center Plan
excerpt: The Virginia Democrat's package would make data centers pay for their own grid upgrades, set federal siting and measurement standards, and protect communities living near AI infrastructure.
body:
• Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) introduced a National Data Center Plan on September 9, 2026: four bills covering siting standards, utility costs, energy and water measurement, and security.
  • The Data Center Fair Share Act would require data centers and other large energy users to pay the full cost of grid upgrades through state-level large-load tariffs; states that refuse would lose federal highway funds.
  • The package responds to backlash in northern Virginia - home to the fourth-largest concentration of data centers in the world - where residents report rising utility bills and transmission lines cutting through neighborhoods.
  • Companion bills would direct the Energy Department to set siting best practices, NIST to standardize energy and water measurement, and DHS, CISA and the Pentagon to craft a defense strategy for surrounding communities.

An Indian-American congressman from the heart of America's data-center capital is pushing a national plan to make the artificial intelligence building boom pay its own way. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, a Democrat representing Virginia's 10th Congressional District, introduced a four-bill National Data Center Plan on September 9 that would require data centers to fund their own energy infrastructure, measure their water and electricity use, and assess impacts on surrounding communities, the environment and national security before building.

The four bills

The Responsible Data Center Siting Act would direct the Secretary of Energy to establish national best practices for locating data centers, weighing energy availability, utility-bill impacts, water and electricity use, the environment, noise, national security, workforce needs and tax revenue. It is co-sponsored by Reps. Mike Quigley (D-IL), Andre Carson (D-IN), Hillary Scholten (D-MI), Veronica Escobar (D-TX), Greg Stanton (D-AZ) and Mike Levin (D-CA), according to Subramanyam's office.

The Data Center Fair Share Act requires data centers and other large energy users to pay the full cost of grid and generation upgrades needed to serve them. States would be required to adopt large-load tariffs ensuring data centers - not residents - pay for their own power, and states that fail to do so would lose access to federal highway funds.

The Data Infrastructure Energy Measurement and Standards Act directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop technical standards for measuring data center energy and water use, so the public and regulators know exactly how much data centers consume.

The Data Infrastructure Risk Reduction Act would require DHS and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, working with the Secretary of Defense, to develop a strategy to protect communities living near data infrastructure - and to shield US data infrastructure from adversaries.

Context & Background

Subramanyam's district sits inside northern Virginia, which hosts the fourth-largest concentration of data centers in the world, with many more on the way as AI-driven demand for compute capacity surges. Residents have complained that transmission lines are being cut through schools and backyards, utility bills are climbing, and development decisions are being made without community input. Elena Schlossberg, executive director of the Coalition to Protect Prince William County, said the region's grid could face catastrophic failure under the industry's power demands, calling Subramanyam's plan a needed step to protect residents, the environment and the grid from irresponsible development.

"Our region is home to the fourth largest concentration of data centers in the world, and many more are on the way. Because of this, our utility bills are up and transmission lines are cutting through our schools and backyards. People are concerned about the future of our community and angry about the impact this will have on noise, the environment, and their property."

— Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.)

Impact & Analysis

The Fair Share Act is the package's sharpest edge: by tying federal highway dollars to large-load tariffs, it would stop residential ratepayers from subsidizing the AI buildout. Consumer Federation of America's Karim D. Marshall called it "a welcome and necessary step," arguing that "consumers shouldn't be forced to subsidize Big Tech through their power bills." The measurement bill fills a genuine gap, Nextgov noted - no common federal standard exists for reporting data-center energy and water use - though the industry is likely to resist the cost-shifting provisions.

Diaspora Angle

The proposal places an Indian-American lawmaker at the center of one of the most consequential technology policy debates of the AI era - how America builds the physical infrastructure its digital economy runs on - giving the diaspora a direct voice in shaping the rules of the AI buildout.

What's Next

The bills, introduced September 9, must clear House committees before any vote - an uphill path with Democrats in the minority. Still, as utility bills rise in data-center-heavy regions nationwide, the Fair Share Act's core idea - that data centers should pay for the grid they consume - is likely to surface in statehouses and future federal legislation regardless of the package's fate.
